name: Melon
lede: Melon is a pale, warm pink with a touch of orange, named for the flesh of a ripe fruit and recorded as a color name since at least 1892.

sections.title: A fruit's color
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* (1930) lists Melon at plate 2, position D 10, and gives 1892 as the earliest use the library finds [1]. The NBS Circular 553 of 1955 places it in ISCC-NBS block 26, with a nearest category of light yellowish pink about 6.3 units away [1]. The swatch here is the dictionary value; an online survey of 2010 used a stronger coral-orange for the same word, so the name covers a wide range [1].

The books tell little of the color itself. Paterson's *Dictionary of Colour* defines the neighboring cantaloupe as a light shade of yellow, after the melon of the same name, which shows that the fruit gives its name to more than one color, depending on the variety [2]. The other color books we hold mention melons only as produce, never as a color [3].

In Japan the library files this swatch's neighborhood with *arazome*, a washed-out crimson dye [1]. Its closest neighbors are [[salmon]], [[peach]] and [[pale-pink]] [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Melon appears in 12 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 0.05%, as photographed [5]. It is rarer than 75% of the named colors [5]. The earliest match is a painting by Correggio of 1515, 377 years before the name's earliest record in our library, so this is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph and not proof of a pigment [5]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [5].
